newsitem.title: CHINA: China poses no threat to U.S., Chinese leader says.
newsitem.headline: China poses no threat to U.S., Chinese leader says.

text.p: China poses no threat to the United States and is eager to see relations improve despite outstanding differences, the head of China's parliament told Republican U.S. Senator Strom Thurmond on Friday.

"Certain differences exist between China and the United States, but compared with the mutual interests of the two countries these differences are partial," the Xinhua news agency quoted Qiao Shi, head of China's National People's Congress or parliament as saying.

"China will pose no threat to the United States and as the 21st century approaches should start from the basic principle of protecting the fundamental interests of the two peoples," Qiao told the 94-year-old congressman, a staunch anti-communist and supporter of Taiwan, which China views as a rebel province.

Qiao was speaking just two months before Chinese President Jiang Zemin is due to visit the United States for a long-awaited summit with President Bill Clinton that is expected to set the seal on a warming of long-fraught Sino-U.S. ties.
"Under new historical conditions, the need for China and the United States to maintain and expand cooperation has not weakened, but continues to increase," Qiao was quoted as saying.

However, Qiao stressed to his staunchly pro-Taiwan visitor the need for the United States to uphold the principles of the three Sino-U.S. joint communiques under which Washington recognises Beijing sovereignty over the island.

Thurmond, who arrived on Thursday for a four-day visit, is president pro tempore of the U.S. Senate and head of its Armed Services committee and has strongly backed U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan, a policy Beijing vigorously opposes.

Thurmond's visit is the latest in a series of trips by U.S. lawmakers to China since late last year when Washington and Beijing began mending fences after ties were strained by disputes over issues such as human rights, trade and the status of Taiwan.
The senator from South Carolina was due to fly to the seaside resort of Beidaihe on Sunday for talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Defence Minister Chi Haotian.

Washington has shown a commitment to boost ties with China, although Beijing has pounced on more conservative views in the United States which advocate containment over engagement as evidence of U.S. suspicion of Asia's strongest communist state.
Beijing has been particularly alarmed by what it sees as signs that Washington may be favouring Taiwan as the island battles to break out of its Beijing-imposed diplomatic isolation.

Communist Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since the two were split at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949 and opposes arms sales to the Nationalist-ruled island as infringing Chinese sovereignty.
Taiwan has bought 150 F-16 fighter jets, batteries of Gulf War-tested Patriot anti-missile missiles and 1,299 shoulder-fired Stinger missiles from the United States despite Beijing's protests.
Taipei says a strong military is needed to defend against Beijing's standing threat to invade if the island abandons its pro-unification policy and declares independence.
